section: 2 From a Gaussian prior to a ridge penalty
text:
2 From a Gaussian prior to a ridge penalty
Consider a linear model 𝒚=X𝜷+𝜺\mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon with 𝜺∼N(𝟎,σ2I)\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2 I) and an independent Gaussian prior on every coefficient, βj∼N(0,τ2)\beta_j\sim N(0,\tau^2). The log posterior is
log⁡p(𝜷∣𝒚)=−12σ2‖𝒚−X𝜷‖2−12τ2‖𝜷‖2+const.
\log p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\mathbf y)
=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\lVert\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2
-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2+\text{const}.

Multiplying by −2σ2-2\sigma^2 shows that maximizing the posterior is the same as minimizing
‖𝒚−X𝜷‖2+λ‖𝜷‖2,λ=σ2τ2.
\lVert\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2,
\qquad
\lambda=\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}.

That is ridge regression. The posterior mode, which for a normal posterior is also the mean, has the closed form
𝜷̂ridge=(X𝖳X+λI)−1X𝖳𝒚,
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}}=\left(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I\right)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y,

and the posterior covariance is σ2(X𝖳X+λI)−1\sigma^2\left(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I\right)^{-1}.
Three consequences follow.

The penalty is a prior. A large λ\lambda means a small prior variance: strong belief that coefficients are near zero. A small λ\lambda means a diffuse prior.
Ridge is a multilevel model. The random-effects model uj∼N(0,τ2)u_j\sim N(0,\tau^2) of Tutorial 4.2 is exactly this prior. The difference is how λ\lambda is chosen: a multilevel model estimates τ2\tau^2 and σ2\sigma^2 by maximum likelihood, whereas ridge regression usually chooses λ\lambda by cross-validation.
Other priors give other penalties. A Laplace (double-exponential) prior gives the lasso’s λ∑j|βj|\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j| penalty, whose posterior mode sets some coefficients exactly to zero.

text:
3 Adjusted plus-minus
A basketball player’s raw plus-minus is the team’s scoring margin while they are on the court. It credits a player for their teammates and debits them for their opponents. Adjusted plus-minus removes that confounding with a regression.
The unit of observation is a stint: a stretch of play during which the ten players on the court do not change. For stint ss, let ysy_s be the home team’s scoring margin per 100 possessions and define
xsj={+1if player j is on the court for the home team,−1if player j is on the court for the away team,0otherwise.
x_{sj}=
\begin{cases}
+1 & \text{if player } j \text{ is on the court for the home team},\\
-1 & \text{if player } j \text{ is on the court for the away team},\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

The model is
ys=∑jxsjβj+εs,Var⁡(εs)=σ2ws,
y_s=\sum_{j}x_{sj}\beta_j+\varepsilon_s,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_s)=\frac{\sigma^2}{w_s},

where wsw_s is the number of possessions in the stint divided by 100, so that longer stints are measured more precisely. The coefficient βj\beta_j is the player’s contribution to the margin per 100 possessions against average teammates and opponents.

3.1 Why least squares fails
Players who share the court constantly, such as a starting lineup, produce nearly identical columns in XX. The matrix X𝖳XX^{\mathsf T}X is then close to singular and the least-squares estimates have enormous variance: two teammates can receive +30+30 and −28-28 when the truth is +1+1 and +1+1. Ridge regression stabilizes the estimates by pulling every coefficient toward zero, which is why the standard method is regularized adjusted plus-minus (RAPM).

Real stint data do not reveal the true player values, so this tutorial uses a simulation in which they are known. Sixty players are divided into six teams of ten. 5 Choosing the penalty
In practice σ2\sigma^2 and τ2\tau^2 are unknown. There are two standard ways to pick λ\lambda.

5.1 Cross-validation
Split the stints into folds, fit on all but one fold, and measure prediction error on the held-out fold. Choose the λ\lambda that predicts unseen stints best.

cross_validate <- function(lambda, folds = 10, seed = 431) {
  set.seed(seed)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(folds), length.out = nrow(sim$X)))
  errors <- sapply(seq_len(folds), function(f) {
    train <- fold != f
    beta <- ridge_closed_form(sim$X[train, ], sim$y[train], lambda, weights[train])
    prediction <- sim$X[!train, ] %*% beta
    sum(weights[!train] * (sim$y[!train] - prediction)^2) / sum(weights[!train])
  })
  mean(errors)
}

lambda_grid <- c(1, 3, 10, 30, 60, 100, 150, 250, 400, 700, 1000)
cv_results <- data.frame(
  lambda = lambda_grid,
  cv_error = sapply(lambda_grid, cross_validate)
)

5.2 Marginal likelihood: the multilevel estimate
The multilevel view treats the player values as random effects and estimates τ2\tau^2 and σ2\sigma^2 by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the margins after integrating the values out. With 𝒚̃=W1/2𝒚\tilde{\mathbf y}=W^{1/2}\mathbf y and X̃=W1/2X\tilde X=W^{1/2}X,
𝒚̃∼N(𝟎,τ2X̃X̃𝖳+σ2I).
\tilde{\mathbf y}\sim N\!\left(\mathbf 0,\ \tau^2\tilde X\tilde X^{\mathsf T}+\sigma^2 I\right).

The determinant and inverse of that S×SS\times S matrix reduce to J×JJ\times J computations through the matrix determinant lemma and the Woodbury identity, which is what makes the calculation cheap.

Xw <- sqrt(weights) * sim$X
yw <- sqrt(weights) * sim$y
XtX <- crossprod(Xw)
Xty <- crossprod(Xw, yw)
S <- length(yw)
J <- ncol(Xw)

marginal_log_likelihood <- function(log_tau, log_sigma) {
  tau2 <- exp(2 * log_tau)
  sigma2 <- exp(2 * log_sigma)
  ratio <- sigma2 / tau2
  inner <- XtX + ratio * diag(J)
  log_det <- (S - J) * log(sigma2) + as.numeric(determinant(sigma2 * diag(J) + tau2 * XtX)$modulus)
  quadratic <- (sum(yw^2) - as.numeric(t(Xty) %*% solve(inner, Xty))) / sigma2
  -0.5 * (log_det + quadratic + S * log(2 * pi))
}

ml_fit <- optim(
  c(log(1), log(20)),
  function(p) -marginal_log_likelihood(p[[1]], p[[2]]),
  method = "BFGS"
)

tau_hat <- exp(ml_fit$par[[1]])
sigma_hat <- exp(ml_fit$par[[2]])
lambda_ml <- sigma_hat^2 / tau_hat^2

data.frame(
  quantity = c("tau (between-player sd)", "sigma (noise sd per 100)", "lambda = sigma^2 / tau^2"),
  estimate = c(tau_hat, sigma_hat, lambda_ml),
  truth = c(sim$true_sd, sim$noise_sd, lambda_known)
) %>%

6 Posterior intervals and rank probabilities
With λ̂\hat\lambda in hand, the posterior for the player values is normal with mean 𝜷̂ridge\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}} and covariance σ̂2(X̃𝖳X̃+λ̂I)−1\hat\sigma^2(\tilde X^{\mathsf T}\tilde X+\hat\lambda I)^{-1}.

posterior_mean <- ridge_closed_form(sim$X, sim$y, lambda_ml, weights)
posterior_cov <- sigma_hat^2 * solve(XtX + lambda_ml * diag(J))
posterior_sd <- sqrt(diag(posterior_cov))

player_table <- data.frame(
  player = names(sim$true_value),
  truth = sim$true_value,
  estimate = posterior_mean,
  sd = posterior_sd,
  lower_95 = posterior_mean - 1.96 * posterior_sd,
  upper_95 = posterior_mean + 1.96 * posterior_sd,
  stints = colSums(sim$X != 0)
)

data.frame(
  coverage_of_true_values = mean(player_table$truth >= player_table$lower_95 & player_table$truth <= player_table$upper_95)
) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

text:
7 RAPM in practice
Production versions of this model differ from the simulation in several ways.

Offense and defense. Each player has two coefficients, one for possessions on offense and one on defense, so the design matrix has two columns per player and the response is points per possession for the offense.
Scale. An NBA season has roughly 30,000 stints and 500 players; several seasons are pooled with a decaying weight on older data. Sparse solvers such as glmnet handle this comfortably.
Informative priors. Instead of shrinking toward zero, the prior mean can be a box-score estimate of the player’s value or the previous season’s RAPM adjusted for aging. The estimate is then 𝜷̂=(X𝖳WX+λI)−1(X𝖳W𝒚+λ𝜷0)\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^{\mathsf T}WX+\lambda I)^{-1}(X^{\mathsf T}W\mathbf y+\lambda\boldsymbol\beta_0), the same formula with a nonzero prior center.
Other sports. Hockey uses the same structure with shifts as stints; soccer versions use player segments between substitutions with expected goals as the response.
Limitations. RAPM measures what happened while a player was on the court relative to replacement lineups. Its precision depends on lineup variety, so players who always play together remain hard to separate, and no penalty can fix that.

10 Key takeaways

Ridge regression is the posterior mode under a Gaussian prior with λ=σ2/τ2\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2.
Adjusted plus-minus needs regularization because shared playing time makes least squares unstable.
The penalty can be chosen by cross-validation or by marginal likelihood; the second is the multilevel estimate.
Posterior intervals and rank probabilities communicate the uncertainty that a ranking hides.

text:
2 Two meanings of probability
A frequentist probability is a long-run frequency: the fraction of times an event would occur under repeated sampling. A Bayesian probability is a degree of belief about any uncertain quantity, including a parameter such as a player’s true shooting percentage. The rules of probability are the same; the difference is what we are willing to assign a probability to.
Bayes’ rule for a parameter θ\theta and data yy is
p(θ∣y)=p(y∣θ)p(θ)p(y)∝p(y∣θ)⏟likelihoodp(θ)⏟prior.
p(\theta\mid y)=\frac{p(y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(y)}
\propto
\underbrace{p(y\mid\theta)}_{\text{likelihood}}\;
\underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{prior}}.

The denominator p(y)=∫p(y∣θ)p(θ)dθp(y)=\int p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta does not depend on θ\theta; it rescales the product to integrate to one. Everything we learn from data is contained in the posterior p(θ∣y)p(\theta\mid y).

title: 4.4 Bayesian Thinking and the Multilevel Connection
text:
3 Beta-binomial: Caitlin Clark’s three-point shooting
Let θ\theta be the probability that a three-point attempt is made. Over nn attempts with ss makes, the likelihood is binomial:
p(s∣θ)=(ns)θs(1−θ)n−s.
p(s\mid\theta)=\binom{n}{s}\theta^{s}(1-\theta)^{n-s}.

A convenient prior is the beta distribution,
p(θ)=θa−1(1−θ)b−1B(a,b),E[θ]=aa+b.
p(\theta)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)},
\qquad
E[\theta]=\frac{a}{a+b}.

Multiplying prior and likelihood gives another beta distribution:
p(θ∣s)∝θs+a−1(1−θ)n−s+b−1⇒θ∣s∼Beta⁡(a+s,b+n−s).
p(\theta\mid s)\propto\theta^{s+a-1}(1-\theta)^{n-s+b-1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta\mid s\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+s,\ b+n-s).

The prior and posterior belong to the same family; the beta is conjugate to the binomial. The hyperparameters act like a prior sample of aa makes and bb misses, and the posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and the observed rate:
E[θ∣s]=a+sa+b+n=a+ba+b+n⋅aa+b+na+b+n⋅sn.
E[\theta\mid s]=\frac{a+s}{a+b+n}
=\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac{a}{a+b}+\frac{n}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac{s}{n}.

3.2 Choosing a prior from the league
A flat prior Beta⁡(1,1)\operatorname{Beta}(1,1) says every percentage from 0 to 1 is equally plausible before seeing data. Nobody believes that about a WNBA player. A better prior comes from the league: the distribution of three-point percentages across players is the natural population for θ\theta.

3.4 Sequential updating
Because the posterior after one game is the prior for the next, we can process the season game by game. The final posterior is the same regardless of the order or grouping of the updates.

  mutate(
    cumulative_makes = cumsum(fg3m),
    cumulative_attempts = cumsum(fg3a),
    a = prior[["a"]] + cumulative_makes,

4 Normal-normal: a passer’s EPA
For a continuous statistic, the conjugate pair is normal prior and normal likelihood. Let y‾j\bar y_j be passer jj’s mean EPA over njn_j attempts.
Here θj\theta_j is the player’s mean EPA, μ\mu is the population mean, τ2\tau^2 is between-player variance, and σ2\sigma^2 is within-player variance. Throughout this tutorial, N(m,v)N(m,v) denotes a normal distribution with mean mm and variance vv. The following update conditions on known μ,τ2,σ2\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2.
y‾j∣θj∼N(θj,σ2/nj),θj∼N(μ,τ2).
\bar y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N\!\left(\theta_j,\ \sigma^2/n_j\right),
\qquad
\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2).

Completing the square in the exponent gives a normal posterior,
θj∣y‾j,μ,τ2,σ2∼N(mj,vj),1vj=1τ2+njσ2,mj=vj(μτ2+njy‾jσ2).
\theta_j\mid\bar y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2\sim N\!\left(m_j,\ v_j\right),
\qquad
\frac{1}{v_j}=\frac{1}{\tau^2}+\frac{n_j}{\sigma^2},
\qquad
m_j=v_j\left(\frac{\mu}{\tau^2}+\frac{n_j\bar y_j}{\sigma^2}\right).

Precisions add, and the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data. Rearranging,
mj=μ+njτ2njτ2+σ2(y‾j−μ).
m_j=\mu+\frac{n_j\tau^2}{n_j\tau^2+\sigma^2}\left(\bar y_j-\mu\right).

This is the shrinkage estimator of Tutorial 4.2 with μ=β0\mu=\beta_0. The multilevel BLUP is the posterior mean of a normal-normal model.

5 Where do the hyperparameters come from?
The prior N(μ,τ2)N(\mu,\tau^2) has its own parameters, and there are three ways to handle them.









Approach

Software

Results depend on the choice

lme4

Fully Bayesian

Stan, rstanarm, brms
Uncertainty in τ2\tau^2 propagates to every player



A model fitted by lme4 has an empirical Bayes interpretation for its group effects. In a Gaussian linear mixed model, the conditional modes equal the conditional means. In a generalized linear mixed model, ranef() returns conditional modes, which generally differ from posterior means. The model structure alone does not determine whether the fitting method is frequentist or Bayesian.

5.1 Averaging over population uncertainty
Let 𝒚\mathbf y denote all observed EPA values and let h=(μ,τ2,σ2)h=(\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2) collect the population parameters. Full Bayes averages the conditional player posterior over the posterior for hh:
p(θj∣𝒚)=∫p(θj∣𝒚,h)p(h∣𝒚)dh.
p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
=\int p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y,h)\,p(h\mid\mathbf y)\,dh.

At each posterior draw, the shrinkage weight changes with the sampled population parameters. The law of total variance makes the extra source of uncertainty explicit:
Var⁡(θj∣𝒚)=Eh∣𝒚[Var(θj∣𝒚,h)]+Var⁡h∣𝒚[E(θj∣𝒚,h)].
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
=E_{h\mid\mathbf y}\!\left[\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y,h)\right]
+\operatorname{Var}_{h\mid\mathbf y}\!\left[E(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y,h)\right].

The first term averages conditional uncertainty. The second measures how conditional means vary across population-parameter draws. This includes uncertainty that a plug-in analysis omits. It does not guarantee that every full Bayesian interval is wider than its empirical Bayes counterpart, because the priors and fitted distributions also differ.

The complete hierarchical model for EPA is
Yij∣θj,σ2∼N(θj,σ2),θj∣μ,τ2∼N(μ,τ2),μ∼N(0,1),τ2∼IG⁡(2,0.04),σ2∼IG⁡(2,4).
\begin{aligned}
Y_{ij}\mid\theta_j,\sigma^2 &\sim N(\theta_j,\sigma^2),\\
\theta_j\mid\mu,\tau^2 &\sim N(\mu,\tau^2),\\
\mu &\sim N(0,1),\\
\tau^2 &\sim\operatorname{IG}(2,0.04),\\
\sigma^2 &\sim\operatorname{IG}(2,4).
\end{aligned}

Here j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,J indexes quarterbacks and i=1,…,nji=1,\ldots,n_j indexes attempts. YijY_{ij} is EPA on an attempt; lowercase yijy_{ij} denotes its observed value. Observations and player effects are conditionally independent at their respective levels.
Define IG⁡(a,b)\operatorname{IG}(a,b) by density proportional to v−a−1exp⁡(−b/v)v^{-a-1}\exp(-b/v) for v>0v>0. Equivalently, 1/v∼Gamma⁡(a,rate=b)1/v\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,\text{rate}=b). The variance priors above have means 0.04 and 4. They give convenient conjugate Gibbs updates and match the teaching model in Tutorial 4.7. They are explicit teaching assumptions, not universal default priors. Tutorial 4.5 uses a different likelihood and an exponential prior on the player standard deviation.
The posterior includes all player means and all unknown population parameters. Full Bayes requires priors for the population mean and residual variance as well as the player variance.

text:
7 Gibbs sampling: repeating the shrinkage update
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) produces a sequence of dependent draws whose stationary distribution is the posterior. After allowing the chain to settle and checking its behavior, we use retained draws to estimate posterior quantities. Finite chains give numerical approximations, even when each update draws exactly from a known distribution.
Gibbs sampling is an MCMC method that repeatedly draws from each parameter’s full conditional: its distribution given the observed data and all other current parameter values. For the Gaussian hierarchy above, one iteration is:

Draw each θj\theta_j using the normal-normal shrinkage update with the current μ,τ2,σ2\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2.
Draw μ\mu conditional on the current player means and player variance.
Draw τ2\tau^2 conditional on the current player means and population mean.
Draw σ2\sigma^2 conditional on the current player means and observed EPA values.

Each iteration revises both player estimates and the population distribution. Pooling strength therefore changes across draws. Integrating population uncertainty is the statistical goal; Gibbs sampling is one way to compute it.






NoteShow the full conditional distributions and R implementation





Let N=∑j=1JnjN=\sum_{j=1}^{J}n_j be the total attempts and y‾j=nj−1∑iyij\bar y_j=n_j^{-1}\sum_i y_{ij} the player average. The symbol ∣⋅\mid\cdot means conditional on the data and all other current parameters. Define conditional variances vj,vμv_j,v_\mu and means mj,mμm_j,m_\mu by
vj=(nj/σ2+1/τ2)−1,mj=vj(njy‾j/σ2+μ/τ2),vμ=(1+J/τ2)−1,mμ=vμ∑jθj/τ2.
\begin{aligned}
v_j&=\left(n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2\right)^{-1},&
m_j&=v_j\left(n_j\bar y_j/\sigma^2+\mu/\tau^2\right),\\
v_\mu&=\left(1+J/\tau^2\right)^{-1},&
m_\mu&=v_\mu\sum_j\theta_j/\tau^2.
\end{aligned}

The updates are
θj∣⋅∼N(mj,vj),μ∣⋅∼N(mμ,vμ),τ2∣⋅∼IG⁡(2+J/2,0.04+12∑j(θj−μ)2),σ2∣⋅∼IG⁡(2+N/2,4+12∑j,i(yij−θj)2).
\begin{aligned}
\theta_j\mid\cdot&\sim N(m_j,v_j),\\
\mu\mid\cdot&\sim N(m_\mu,v_\mu),\\
\tau^2\mid\cdot&\sim\operatorname{IG}\!\left(2+J/2,\ 0.04+\tfrac12\sum_j(\theta_j-\mu)^2\right),\\
\sigma^2\mid\cdot&\sim\operatorname{IG}\!\left(2+N/2,\ 4+\tfrac12\sum_{j,i}(y_{ij}-\theta_j)^2\right).
\end{aligned}

The player update repeats the familiar shrinkage rule. The term 1 in the population-mean precision comes from the N(0,1)N(0,1) prior. The inverse-gamma updates use R’s gamma rate, not its scale.
gibbs_epa <- function(stats, seed, iterations = 4000, warmup = 1500) {
  stopifnot(iterations > warmup, all(stats$n > 0))
  set.seed(seed)
  J <- nrow(stats)
  theta <- stats$raw
  mu <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.3)
  tau2 <- runif(1, 0.02, 0.15)
  sigma2 <- runif(1, 2, 6)
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, iterations - warmup, J + 3,
                dimnames = list(NULL, c(as.character(stats$passer),
                                      "mu", "tau", "sigma")))
  for (iteration in seq_len(iterations)) {
    v <- 1 / (stats$n / sigma2 + 1 / tau2)
    m <- v * (stats$sy / sigma2 + mu / tau2)
    theta <- rnorm(J, m, sqrt(v))
    v_mu <- 1 / (1 + J / tau2)
    mu <- rnorm(1, v_mu * sum(theta) / tau2, sqrt(v_mu))
    tau2 <- 1 / rgamma(1, 2 + J / 2,
                       rate = 0.04 + sum((theta - mu)^2) / 2)
    sse <- sum(stats$sy2 - 2 * theta * stats$sy + stats$n * theta^2)
    sigma2 <- 1 / rgamma(1, 2 + sum(stats$n) / 2,
                         rate = 4 + max(sse, 0) / 2)
    if (iteration > warmup)
      out[iteration - warmup, ] <- c(theta, mu, sqrt(tau2), sqrt(sigma2))
  }
  out
}
The function uses the sufficient statistics n, sy, sy2, and raw: attempt count, sum of EPA, sum of squared EPA, and mean EPA. Its output stores standard deviations tau and sigma, although its internal updates sample variances.

9 Key takeaways

A posterior is prior times likelihood, renormalized; conjugate pairs make the update a formula.
The beta-binomial posterior mean weights the prior mean and observed rate by their effective sample sizes.
The normal-normal posterior mean is the multilevel shrinkage estimate, and its variance is the conditional variance of the BLUP.

A fully Bayesian model adds priors on the variance parameters and integrates over them, so uncertainty in the population distribution contributes to inference.
Gibbs sampling repeats conditional updates and averages over unknown population parameters. Stan uses HMC/NUTS to sample more general models.

2 Three ways to estimate a passer’s EPA
Tutorial 4.1 showed that the observed EPA per attempt is a noisy estimate of ability. There are three natural estimators.
Complete pooling ignores the passer entirely and uses the league mean for everyone:
θ̂jpool=y‾.
\hat\theta_j^{\text{pool}}=\bar y.

No pooling uses each passer’s own mean:
θ̂jnone=y‾j.
\hat\theta_j^{\text{none}}=\bar y_j.

Partial pooling uses a compromise, and the multilevel model tells us the weight.

no_pooling <- passes %>%
  group_by(passer) %>%
  summarize(attempts = n(), epa_mean = mean(qb_epa), .groups = "drop")

complete_pooling

title: 4.2 Multilevel Models with Varying Intercepts
text:
3 The two-level model
At level one, each attempt is the passer’s mean plus noise:
yij=β0j+εij,εij∼N(0,σ2).
y_{ij}=\beta_{0j}+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2).

At level two, each passer’s mean is the league mean plus a passer deviation:
β0j=β0+uj,uj∼N(0,τ2).
\beta_{0j}=\beta_0+u_j,
\qquad
u_j\sim N(0,\tau^2).

Substituting gives the composite model
yij=β0+uj+εij.
y_{ij}=\beta_0+u_j+\varepsilon_{ij}.

Here β0\beta_0 is a fixed effect: one unknown constant for the whole league. The uju_j are random effects: they are treated as draws from a distribution whose variance τ2\tau^2 is estimated. The word “random” does not mean the passers were sampled at random. It means we model the population of passer effects with a distribution and borrow strength across them.

3.1 Laird-Ware form
For every observation stacked into a vector 𝒚\mathbf y of length NN,
𝒚=X𝜷+Z𝒖+𝜺,𝒖∼N(𝟎,G),𝜺∼N(𝟎,R),
\mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+Z\mathbf u+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,
\qquad
\mathbf u\sim N(\mathbf 0,G),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N(\mathbf 0,R),

where XX is the N×pN\times p fixed-effect design matrix, ZZ is the N×JN\times J random-effect design matrix with one indicator column per passer, G=τ2IJG=\tau^2 I_J, and R=σ2INR=\sigma^2 I_N. Marginally,
𝒚∼N(X𝜷,ZGZ𝖳+R).
\mathbf y\sim N\!\left(X\boldsymbol\beta,\ ZGZ^{\mathsf T}+R\right).

Two attempts by the same passer share the passer’s uju_j, so their covariance is τ2\tau^2; attempts by different passers are independent. This marginal covariance is what maximum likelihood fits.

5 Shrinkage: the estimate of each passer’s effect
Conditional on the variance components, the best estimate of uju_j is a weighted compromise between the passer’s own mean and the fixed intercept:
ûj=njτ2njτ2+σ2(y‾j−β̂0)=wj(y‾j−β̂0).
\hat u_j=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{n_j\tau^2+\sigma^2}\left(\bar y_j-\hat\beta_0\right)
=w_j\left(\bar y_j-\hat\beta_0\right).

The weight wjw_j is the reliability from Tutorial 4.1. A passer with many attempts keeps most of their observed deviation; a passer with few attempts is pulled almost all the way to the league mean.

5.1 Derivation
Treat uju_j as unknown with distribution N(0,τ2)N(0,\tau^2) and the passer’s mean as data with y‾j∣uj∼N(β0+uj,σ2/nj)\bar y_j\mid u_j\sim N(\beta_0+u_j,\ \sigma^2/n_j). Bayes’ rule with a normal prior and normal likelihood gives a normal posterior whose mean is precision-weighted:
E[uj∣y‾j]=njσ2(y‾j−β0)+1τ2⋅0njσ2+1τ2=njτ2njτ2+σ2(y‾j−β0).
E[u_j\mid \bar y_j]
=\frac{\dfrac{n_j}{\sigma^2}\left(\bar y_j-\beta_0\right)+\dfrac{1}{\tau^2}\cdot 0}{\dfrac{n_j}{\sigma^2}+\dfrac{1}{\tau^2}}
=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{n_j\tau^2+\sigma^2}\left(\bar y_j-\beta_0\right).

The estimator is called the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) in the mixed-model literature and the posterior mean in the Bayesian literature. Tutorial 4.4 returns to this identity.

6 Estimation: ML and REML
The variance components are estimated by maximizing the marginal likelihood of 𝒚\mathbf y after integrating out 𝒖\mathbf u. There are two versions.

Maximum likelihood (ML) maximizes the full marginal likelihood. Variance estimates are biased downward because the fixed effects are estimated from the same data.
Restricted maximum likelihood (REML) maximizes the likelihood of linear contrasts of 𝒚\mathbf y that do not depend on 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta. This removes the bias, in the same way that dividing by n−1n-1 instead of nn corrects the sample variance.

lmer() uses REML by default. Use ML (REML = FALSE) when comparing models with different fixed effects by likelihood ratio, because REML likelihoods are not comparable across fixed-effect specifications.

epa_ml <- lmer(qb_epa ~ 1 + (1 | passer), data = passes, REML = FALSE)

data.frame(

  tau = c(

    as.data.frame(VarCorr(epa_ml))$sdcor[1]

  sigma = c(sigma(epa_fit), sigma(epa_ml))

title: 4.2 Multilevel Models with Varying Intercepts
text:
9 Key takeaways

A multilevel model estimates the population variance of player effects and uses it to weight each player’s data against the league.
The random-effect estimate is the observed deviation multiplied by the reliability njτ2/(njτ2+σ2)n_j\tau^2/(n_j\tau^2+\sigma^2).
The intraclass correlation measures how much of per-play variance is between players.
REML corrects the small-sample bias of variance estimates; ML is needed for comparing fixed-effect specifications.
The same structure extends to binary outcomes through a GLMM.

title: Lecture 4: Player Performance Evaluation
text:
How much of a player’s measured performance is the player, and how much is the situation, the teammates, the opponents, and chance?
Every box-score statistic is an average over a limited number of plays. A quarterback with a 72% completion rate over 40 attempts and a quarterback with a 68% rate over 560 attempts are not equally well measured, and neither number separates the passer from the receivers who caught the ball or the defenses that allowed it. This lecture builds a set of tools for that problem:

Multilevel models treat each player as one group in a population of players and estimate how much of the observed variation is signal. The result is partial pooling: every player’s estimate is pulled toward the league average by an amount that depends on how much we know about that player.
Bayesian inference makes the same idea explicit. A prior distribution describes the population, the data update it, and the posterior describes what we believe about each player and how uncertain we are.
The connection is partial pooling through a population distribution. ML or REML estimates population parameters and gives group estimates with an empirical Bayes interpretation. A fully Bayesian model assigns priors to all unknown parameters and integrates their uncertainty. Gaussian conditional means coincide with mixed-model predictions under matched assumptions, but a logistic mixed-model mode need not equal a posterior mean.

title: 4.1 Player Evaluation and the Problem of Small Samples
text:
4 Signal plus noise
Write the observed mean as ability plus sampling error,
y‾j=θj+εj,εj∼(0,σ2/nj),
\bar y_j=\theta_j+\varepsilon_j,
\qquad
\varepsilon_j\sim\left(0,\ \sigma^2/n_j\right),

where σ2\sigma^2 is the variance of a single attempt’s outcome. Across the population of players, let abilities vary with mean μ\mu and variance τ2\tau^2. Then
Var⁡(y‾j)=τ2⏟signal+σ2/nj⏟noise.
\operatorname{Var}(\bar y_j)=\underbrace{\tau^2}_{\text{signal}}+\underbrace{\sigma^2/n_j}_{\text{noise}}.

The reliability of a player’s average is the share of its variance that is signal,
Rj=τ2τ2+σ2/nj=njnj+σ2/τ2.
R_j=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j}=\frac{n_j}{n_j+\sigma^2/\tau^2}.

The ratio σ2/τ2\sigma^2/\tau^2 is the number of attempts at which reliability equals one half. Beyond that point, the average is more signal than noise.

4.1 Estimate the components from data
For a binary outcome, the within-player variance is approximately p‾(1−p‾)\bar p(1-\bar p). Because Var⁡(y‾j)=τ2+σ2/nj\operatorname{Var}(\bar y_j)=\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j, a method-of-moments estimate of τ2\tau^2 subtracts the average noise from the observed variance of player means.

eligible <- qbs %>% filter(attempts >= 50)

sigma2_completion <- mean(eligible$completion_rate * (1 - eligible$completion_rate))
tau2_completion <- estimate_tau2_moments(
  eligible$completion_rate,
  eligible$attempts,
  sigma2_completion
)

sigma2_epa <- mean(eligible$epa_sd^2)
tau2_epa <- estimate_tau2_moments(
  eligible$epa_per_attempt,
  eligible$attempts,
  sigma2_epa
)

  statistic = c("completion rate", "EPA per attempt"),
  within_variance = c(sigma2_completion, sigma2_epa),
  between_variance = c(tau2_completion, tau2_epa),
  between_sd = sqrt(c(tau2_completion, tau2_epa)),
  attempts_for_half_reliability = c(
    sigma2_completion / tau2_completion,
    sigma2_epa / tau2_epa

4.2 Check the decomposition with split halves
Split halves means dividing each passer’s included attempts into two interleaved samples: attempts 1, 3, 5, and so on form the odd half; attempts 2, 4, 6, and so on form the even half. Calculate a completion rate or mean EPA for each half. Then correlate the two sets of averages across passers, rather than correlating individual attempts within one passer.
To see the connection to reliability, suppose each half contains mm attempts per passer and measures the same underlying mean θj\theta_j:
Y‾j,o=θj+εj,o,Y‾j,e=θj+εj,e.
\bar Y_{j,o}=\theta_j+\varepsilon_{j,o},
\qquad
\bar Y_{j,e}=\theta_j+\varepsilon_{j,e}.

Here jj indexes passers, oo and ee label the odd and even halves, Y‾\bar Y denotes a random half-sample average, and ε\varepsilon its sampling error. Assume zero conditional error means, errors conditionally independent given θj\theta_j, common error variance σ2/m\sigma^2/m, and between-passer variance Var⁡(θj)=τ2\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j)=\tau^2. The halves share the player mean, but their sampling errors do not covary. Thus,
Cov⁡(Y‾j,o,Y‾j,e)=τ2,Var⁡(Y‾j,o)=Var⁡(Y‾j,e)=τ2+σ2/m.
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y_{j,o},\bar Y_{j,e})&=\tau^2,\\
\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_{j,o})=\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_{j,e})&=\tau^2+\sigma^2/m.
\end{aligned}

Dividing the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations gives the population correlation:
Corr⁡(Y‾j,o,Y‾j,e)=τ2τ2+σ2/m=Rhalf,
\operatorname{Corr}(\bar Y_{j,o},\bar Y_{j,e})
=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2/m}
=R_{\mathrm{half}},

where RhalfR_{\mathrm{half}} is the reliability of an average over mm attempts. This follows from the variance assumptions without requiring normality. The observed correlation can differ because of sampling variation, changing context, or dependent attempts. For completion rates, the common noise variance is also an approximation.

title: 4.1 Player Evaluation and the Problem of Small Samples
text:
5 Regression to the mean
Reliability is also the slope of the best linear prediction of a player’s underlying mean from the observed average:
θ̂j=μ+Rj(y‾j−μ),Rj=τ2τ2+σ2/nj.
\hat\theta_j=\mu+R_j(\bar y_j-\mu),
\qquad
R_j=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j}.

Here θj\theta_j is the underlying player mean, θ̂j\hat\theta_j its estimate, y‾j\bar y_j the observed average over njn_j attempts, and μ\mu the population mean. The variances τ2\tau^2 and σ2\sigma^2 describe between-player variation and per-attempt sampling noise. Under the normal-normal model with these population parameters fixed, this predictor is exactly the conditional mean E(θj∣Y‾j=y‾j)E(\theta_j\mid\bar Y_j=\bar y_j). For completion rates, the common-variance Gaussian model is an approximation to binomial sampling.
If the observed average is d=y‾j−μd=\bar y_j-\mu above the population mean, the predicted player mean is only RjdR_jd above it. With stable ability and zero-mean future sampling errors, the Gaussian model also predicts a future average RjdR_jd above the population mean. This is regression to the mean: the expected deviation is smaller even though the player’s ability has not changed. A realized future average can still be higher or lower.






NoteShow the full derivation of regression to the mean





1. Specify the sampling model.
For player jj, let Y‾j\bar Y_j denote the random average before the data are observed, and let y‾j\bar y_j denote its observed value. Write
Y‾j=θj+εj,
\bar Y_j=\theta_j+\varepsilon_j,

where εj\varepsilon_j is the error in the sample average, rather than the error on a single attempt. Treat the positive attempt count njn_j as fixed and assume
E(θj)=μ,Var⁡(θj)=τ2,E(εj∣θj)=0,Var⁡(εj∣θj)=σ2/nj.
\begin{aligned}
E(\theta_j)&=\mu, & \operatorname{Var}(\theta_j)&=\tau^2,\\
E(\varepsilon_j\mid\theta_j)&=0, &
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_j\mid\theta_j)&=\sigma^2/n_j.
\end{aligned}

The sampling variance σ2/nj\sigma^2/n_j follows when attempts are conditionally independent and each has conditional variance σ2\sigma^2. Assume finite variances with τ2>0\tau^2>0 and σ2>0\sigma^2>0.
For completion rates, conditionally independent attempts with the same probability θj\theta_j instead give an exact binomial model: Sj∣θj∼Binomial⁡(nj,θj)S_j\mid\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,\theta_j) and Y‾j=Sj/nj\bar Y_j=S_j/n_j, where SjS_j is the completion count. Thus E(Y‾j∣θj)=θjE(\bar Y_j\mid\theta_j)=\theta_j and the zero conditional error mean is exact. Its conditional error variance is θj(1−θj)/nj\theta_j(1-\theta_j)/n_j; replacing the numerator by common σ2\sigma^2 is the approximation used here.
2. Compute the mean, variance, and covariance.
By iterated expectation, E(εj)=0E(\varepsilon_j)=0, so E(Y‾j)=μE(\bar Y_j)=\mu. Also,
E(θjεj)=E{θjE(εj∣θj)}=0,
E(\theta_j\varepsilon_j)
=E\{\theta_jE(\varepsilon_j\mid\theta_j)\}=0,

which gives Cov⁡(θj,εj)=0\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_j,\varepsilon_j)=0. The law of total variance gives Var⁡(εj)=σ2/nj\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_j)=\sigma^2/n_j. Therefore,
Var⁡(Y‾j)=Var⁡(θj)+Var⁡(εj)=τ2+σ2/nj,Cov⁡(θj,Y‾j)=Cov⁡(θj,θj+εj)=τ2.
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_j)
&=\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j)+\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_j)
=\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j,\\
\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_j,\bar Y_j)
&=\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_j,\theta_j+\varepsilon_j)
=\tau^2.
\end{aligned}

3. Find the best linear predictor.
Consider a predictor a+bY‾ja+b\bar Y_j, where aa is an intercept and bb is a slope. Choose them to minimize the mean squared prediction error
L(a,b)=E{(θj−a−bY‾j)2}.
L(a,b)=E\{(\theta_j-a-b\bar Y_j)^2\}.

For any fixed bb, differentiating with respect to aa gives
∂L∂a=−2E(θj−a−bY‾j)=0,a=μ−bμ.
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}
=-2E(\theta_j-a-b\bar Y_j)=0,
\qquad a=\mu-b\mu.

Substitute this intercept and expand the centered squared error:
L(μ−bμ,b)=τ2−2bCov⁡(θj,Y‾j)+b2Var⁡(Y‾j).
L(\mu-b\mu,b)
=\tau^2-2b\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_j,\bar Y_j)
+b^2\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_j).

Differentiating with respect to bb yields
−2Cov⁡(θj,Y‾j)+2bVar⁡(Y‾j)=0,
-2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_j,\bar Y_j)
+2b\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_j)=0,

so the minimizing slope is
b=Cov⁡(θj,Y‾j)Var⁡(Y‾j)=τ2τ2+σ2/nj=Rj.
b=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_j,\bar Y_j)}{\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_j)}
=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j}
=R_j.

The second derivative is 2Var⁡(Y‾j)>02\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_j)>0, confirming a minimum. After observing Y‾j=y‾j\bar Y_j=\bar y_j, the predictor becomes
θ̂j=μ+Rj(y‾j−μ).
\boxed{\hat\theta_j=\mu+R_j(\bar y_j-\mu)}.

Reliability is the regression slope because the covariance equals the signal variance, while the observed variance contains both signal and noise. This linear prediction result uses the stated moments and does not require normality.
4. State when the predictor is the exact conditional mean.
If we additionally assume
θj∼N(μ,τ2),Y‾j∣θj∼N(θj,σ2/nj),
\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2),
\qquad
\bar Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N(\theta_j,\sigma^2/n_j),

then θj\theta_j and Y‾j\bar Y_j are jointly normal. Their conditional mean is linear, giving
E(θj∣Y‾j=y‾j)=μ+Rj(y‾j−μ).
E(\theta_j\mid\bar Y_j=\bar y_j)
=\mu+R_j(\bar y_j-\mu).

Without this additional distributional assumption, the best linear predictor need not equal the conditional mean. The normal-normal posterior is derived in Tutorial 4.4. All displayed conditional formulas here treat μ\mu, τ2\tau^2, and σ2\sigma^2 as fixed; substituting estimates is a separate step.
5. Connect the result to future performance.
Let Y‾̃j=θj+ε̃j\widetilde{\bar Y}_j=\theta_j+\widetilde\varepsilon_j denote an average over future attempts, where the player mean is unchanged and E(ε̃j∣θj,Y‾j)=0E(\widetilde\varepsilon_j\mid\theta_j,\bar Y_j)=0. Iterated conditional expectation gives
E(Y‾̃j∣Y‾j=y‾j)=E{E(Y‾̃j∣θj,Y‾j=y‾j)∣Y‾j=y‾j}=E(θj∣Y‾j=y‾j)=μ+Rj(y‾j−μ).
\begin{aligned}
E(\widetilde{\bar Y}_j\mid\bar Y_j=\bar y_j)
&=E\{E(\widetilde{\bar Y}_j\mid\theta_j,\bar Y_j=\bar y_j)\mid\bar Y_j=\bar y_j\}\\
&=E(\theta_j\mid\bar Y_j=\bar y_j)\\
&=\mu+R_j(\bar y_j-\mu).
\end{aligned}

The last equality uses the normal-normal model. Since 0<Rj<10<R_j<1, the expected future average is closer to μ\mu whenever y‾j≠μ\bar y_j\ne\mu. This is an expectation across possible future outcomes, not a guarantee about the next observed average.

6 Context: not every pass is equally hard
Sampling error is only one problem. A screen pass thrown 2 yards and a deep ball thrown 35 yards under pressure have different completion probabilities regardless of the passer. A raw completion rate rewards quarterbacks who throw short.

passes %>%
  mutate(air_bin = cut(air_yards, breaks = c(-15, 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 70))) %>%
  group_by(air_bin) %>%
  summarize(attempts = n(), completion_rate = mean(complete), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(air_bin, completion_rate, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = "#03a9e6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(size = attempts), color = "#03a9e6") +
  labs(x = "Air yards", y = "Completion rate", size = "Attempts") +
  theme_minimal()




Observed completion rate by air yards. Longer throws are completed less often for every passer.





6.1 An expectation model
The standard remedy is to model the completion probability from the situation and then compare each outcome with its expectation. Let 𝒙i\mathbf{x}_i collect pre-throw features of attempt ii: air yards, pass location, whether the passer was hit, receiver position, down, distance, field position, and formation. A logistic regression gives
p̂i=P(yi=1∣𝒙i)=σ(β0+𝒙i𝖳𝜷),σ(z)=11+e−z.
\hat p_i=P(y_i=1\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\sigma\!\left(\beta_0+\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta\right),
\qquad
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.

The per-attempt residual is completion percentage over expectation,
CPOEi=yi−p̂i,
\mathrm{CPOE}_i=y_i-\hat p_i,

and a player’s CPOE is the average of those residuals over their attempts.

)

title: 4.1 Player Evaluation and the Problem of Small Samples
text:
7 Residual allocation
CPOE averages residuals by passer. That step contains a modeling assumption: everything the expectation model cannot explain is credited to the quarterback. Consider what else is in a residual:

the receiver, who ran the route, created separation, and caught or dropped the ball;
the defense, whose coverage and pass rush are only partly captured by qb_hit;
the offensive line and scheme; and
chance.

A quarterback who throws to an elite receiver against weak defenses accumulates positive residuals that are only partly theirs. Averaging residuals is a residual allocation rule, and it allocates all of the residual to one party.






ImportantTwo separate problems



Sampling noise and credit assignment are different problems with different remedies. Shrinkage addresses the first. Modeling the passer, receiver, and defense together addresses the second. Tutorials 4.2 and 4.3 build a single model that does both.

title: 4.1 Player Evaluation and the Problem of Small Samples
text:
8 Practice

A passer has 30 attempts and a 77% completion rate. Using the estimates above, what is the reliability of that rate and the expected ability?
Why is σ2/τ2\sigma^2/\tau^2 measured in attempts?
Suppose the expectation model included a passer indicator. Why would CPOE then be zero for every passer?
Name two sources of variation that a residual attributes to the quarterback but that the quarterback does not control.

title: 4.1 Player Evaluation and the Problem of Small Samples
text:
9 Key takeaways

An observed average is ability plus noise, and the noise share depends on attempts.
Reliability τ2/(τ2+σ2/n)\tau^2/(\tau^2+\sigma^2/n) is both the signal share and the regression slope toward the mean.
An expectation model removes throw difficulty and produces a residual metric such as CPOE.
Averaging residuals by player assumes the player owns the whole residual; a multilevel model relaxes that assumption.

2 Level-one covariates
Tutorial 4.1 built an expectation model and then averaged residuals by passer. A multilevel model does both steps at once. With level-one covariates 𝒙ij\mathbf x_{ij} describing attempt ii by passer jj,
logit⁡P(yij=1)=β0j+𝒙ij𝖳𝜷,β0j=β0+uj,uj∼N(0,τ2).
\operatorname{logit}P(y_{ij}=1)=\beta_{0j}+\mathbf x_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
\beta_{0j}=\beta_0+u_j,
\qquad
u_j\sim N(0,\tau^2).

The fixed coefficients 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta describe throw difficulty. The random intercept uju_j is the passer’s completion ability after accounting for the throws they attempted. Both are estimated jointly, so the passer effects and the difficulty model inform each other.

  data = passes,
  family = binomial()
)

with_covariates <- glmer(

    (1 | passer),
  data = passes,
  family = binomial()
)

    as.data.frame(VarCorr(intercept_only))$sdcor,
    as.data.frame(VarCorr(with_covariates))$sdcor

) %>%

3 A level-two covariate
A level-two covariate describes the passer rather than the attempt. In the level-two equation,
β0j=γ0+γ1wj+uj,
\beta_{0j}=\gamma_0+\gamma_1 w_j+u_j,

where wjw_j is a passer-level variable and uju_j is now the deviation from what wjw_j predicts. Examples in practice are age, experience, and draft position. Here we use a contextual variable available in the data: the passer’s average air yards, which measures how aggressively they throw.

passes <- passes %>%
  group_by(passer) %>%
  mutate(passer_mean_air = mean(air_yards)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(passer_air_z = (passer_mean_air - mean(passer_mean_air)) / sd(passer_mean_air))

with_level_two <- glmer(
  complete ~ air_yards_z + passer_air_z + qb_hit + pass_location +
    receiver_position + (1 | passer),
  data = passes,
  family = binomial()
)

summary(with_level_two)$coefficients %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  filter(term %in% c("air_yards_z", "passer_air_z")) %>%

4 Varying slopes
So far every passer shares the same air-yards coefficient. Perhaps some passers lose accuracy faster with depth than others. A varying-slope model lets each passer have both an intercept and a slope:
logit⁡P(yij=1)=β0j+β1jxij+⋯,(β0jβ1j)=(β0β1)+(u0ju1j),(u0ju1j)∼N(𝟎,Σ),
\operatorname{logit}P(y_{ij}=1)=\beta_{0j}+\beta_{1j}x_{ij}+\cdots,
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{0j}\\ \beta_{1j}\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\ \beta_1\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}u_{0j}\\ u_{1j}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}u_{0j}\\ u_{1j}\end{pmatrix}
\sim N\!\left(\mathbf 0,\ \Sigma\right),

with
Σ=(τ02ρτ0τ1ρτ0τ1τ12).
\Sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1\\
\rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix}.

The correlation ρ\rho asks whether passers who are better on average (large u0ju_{0j}) are also better or worse on deep throws (large or small u1ju_{1j}).

WarningSingular fits

title: 4.3 Covariates, Varying Slopes, and Crossed Effects
text:
5 Nested and crossed structures
Grouping factors can relate to each other in two ways.
Nested. Each level of the inner factor belongs to exactly one level of the outer factor. Attempts within games within a passer are nested: a game-by-passer combination belongs to one passer. In lme4, (1 | passer / game_id) expands to (1 | passer) + (1 | passer:game_id).
Crossed. Levels of one factor combine with many levels of another. Each pass has a passer, a receiver, and a defense, and the same receiver catches passes from several passers while the same defense faces every passer it plays. Crossed effects are written as separate terms, (1 | passer) + (1 | receiver) + (1 | defteam).
The crossed model is
logit⁡P(yi=1)=β0+𝒙i𝖳𝜷+uq(i)+vr(i)+dk(i),
\operatorname{logit}P(y_i=1)=\beta_0+\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+u_{q(i)}+v_{r(i)}+d_{k(i)},

where q(i)q(i), r(i)r(i), and k(i)k(i) index the passer, receiver, and defense on attempt ii, and
uq∼N(0,τq2),vr∼N(0,τr2),dk∼N(0,τd2).
u_q\sim N(0,\tau_q^2),\qquad v_r\sim N(0,\tau_r^2),\qquad d_k\sim N(0,\tau_d^2).

Every pass now contributes to three effects at once. This is the multilevel answer to the residual-allocation problem: the residual is shared among the parties according to how consistently each one is associated with success.

crossed <- glmer(
  complete ~ air_yards_z + qb_hit + pass_location + receiver_position +
    (1 | passer) + (1 | receiver) + (1 | defteam),
  data = passes,
  family = binomial()
)

as.data.frame(VarCorr(crossed)) %>%
  select(grp, sdcor) %>%

6 Uncertainty in variance components
Standard errors for fixed effects come from the curvature of the log-likelihood and are reported by summary(). Variance components are different: their sampling distributions are skewed and bounded at zero, so a symmetric standard error is a poor summary. The standard remedy is a parametric bootstrap:

record the statistics of interest; and
repeat and read off percentiles.

text:
2 The player-effect model from Tutorial 4.2
For attempt ii by quarterback jj, let Yij=1Y_{ij}=1 for a completion and Yij=0Y_{ij}=0 otherwise. The model is
Yij∣α,uj∼Bernoulli⁡(θj),θj=logit⁡−1(α+uj),uj∣τ∼N(0,τ2),α∼N(0,2.52),τ∼Exponential⁡(rate=1).
\begin{aligned}
Y_{ij}\mid\alpha,u_j&\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta_j),\\
\theta_j&=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha+u_j),\\
u_j\mid\tau&\sim N(0,\tau^2),\\
\alpha&\sim N(0,2.5^2),\\
\tau&\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(\text{rate}=1).
\end{aligned}








Symbol
Meaning

Quarterback index, with JJ quarterbacks in training data

Attempt within a quarterback

Quarterback completion probability under this model

Population intercept on the log-odds scale


uju_j
Quarterback deviation on the log-odds scale

Population standard deviation of quarterback deviations



The inverse logit is logit⁡−1(a)=1/(1+e−a)\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a)=1/(1+e^{-a}) for a real number aa. Normal notation uses variance as its second argument. Stan’s normal() instead takes a standard deviation, so normal(0, 2.5) implements N(0,2.52)N(0,2.5^2).
Attempts are conditionally independent given the player probabilities, and player effects are conditionally independent given τ\tau. This intercept-only model assumes each quarterback’s probability stays constant over the modeled period. It describes completion rates for the filtered pass sample, without adjusting for pass difficulty, receivers, or defenses.
The likelihood and player distribution are the same as in 4.2. The explicit priors for α\alpha and τ\tau complete the Bayesian hierarchy. The posterior jointly describes the intercept, player effects, and population spread. The prior τ∼Exponential⁡(1)\tau\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(1) has density e−τe^{-\tau} for τ>0\tau>0 and mean 1. It permits small player variation while reducing prior weight on large standard deviations. The constants above are teaching choices that warrant sensitivity checks.

2.1 Why Stan is useful
The logistic hierarchy has no simple conjugate posterior formula. Stan computes dependent draws representing its joint posterior using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Its default sampling method is Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) through the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), which uses derivatives of the log posterior to explore it. Stan adapts sampling settings during warmup; NUTS chooses trajectory lengths during sampling. It does not run the Gaussian Gibbs updates from 4.4. Stan sampling documentation
For a posterior quantity qq and MM retained joint draws q(1),…,q(M)q^{(1)},\ldots,q^{(M)},
E(q∣𝒚)≈1M∑m=1Mq(m),
E(q\mid\mathbf y)\approx\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}q^{(m)},

where 𝒚\mathbf y denotes the training outcomes. Quantiles of these draws give credible intervals. Dependence among draws makes the effective sample size smaller than the raw draw count in many cases.

3 Training games and held-out games
We fit games through Week 10 and reserve later games for prediction. Whole games stay together. We restrict the prediction example to quarterbacks seen in training, so their player effects already have posteriors. Predicting an unseen quarterback would require drawing a new player effect from the population distribution.
Because there are no attempt-level covariates, we can aggregate attempts within each quarterback-game without losing likelihood information about the parameters. Let SgS_g be completions and ngn_g attempts for quarterback-game row gg. If j(g)j(g) identifies its quarterback, then
Sg∣α,𝒖∼Binomial⁡(ng,θj(g)).
S_g\mid\alpha,\mathbf u\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_g,\theta_{j(g)}).

Here 𝒖=(u1,…,uJ)\mathbf u=(u_1,\ldots,u_J) is the vector of player effects. The game is an aggregation unit, not an added random effect. The binomial likelihood differs from the attempt-level Bernoulli likelihood only by combinatorial factors that do not depend on the parameters. This aggregation would generally fail if completion probabilities varied within a row because of covariates.

text:
4 Custom Stan through cmdstanr

4.1 The complete Stan program
The file R/completion_player.stan contains the complete model. It writes uj=τzju_j=\tau z_j with zj∼N(0,1)z_j\sim N(0,1). This non-centered parameterization represents the same player distribution while often helping sampling when player information is weak.
data {
  int<lower=1> J;                         // Quarterbacks in training data
  int<lower=1> G;                         // Training quarterback-game rows
  array[G] int<lower=1> n;                // Attempts per row
  array[G] int<lower=0> s;                // Completions per row
  array[G] int<lower=1, upper=J> qb;       // Quarterback index
  int<lower=1> G_test;                    // Held-out quarterback-game rows
  array[G_test] int<lower=1> n_test;
  array[G_test] int<lower=1, upper=J> qb_test;
}
parameters {
  real alpha;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  vector[J] z;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[J] u = tau * z;
  vector[J] theta = inv_logit(alpha + u);
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  tau ~ exponential(1);
  z ~ std_normal();
  s ~ binomial_logit(n, alpha + u[qb]);
}
generated quantities {
  array[G] int s_rep;
  array[G_test] int s_test_rep;
  for (g in 1:G)
    s_rep[g] = binomial_rng(n[g], theta[qb[g]]);
  for (g in 1:G_test)
    s_test_rep[g] = binomial_rng(n_test[g], theta[qb_test[g]]);
}

G and G_test count training and test quarterback-game rows. J counts training quarterbacks. n and s are training attempts and completions, and qb maps each row to a player index. n_test and qb_test supply the prediction settings. s_rep and s_test_rep are simulated completion counts. There is no test-outcome likelihood.


4.2 Data list and fitting call

  J = length(players), G = nrow(train),
  n = train$attempts, s = train$completions,
  qb = as.integer(train$passer),

The code below performs a new fit. The rendered tutorial reads verified saved results so it opens without recompiling. Run the complete script R/fit_completion_stan.R from the Lecture 4 folder to rebuild both Bayesian fits and their predictions. cmdstanr requires an installed CmdStan and a working C++ toolchain. On Windows, follow the CmdStanR toolchain instructions. CmdStanR installation guide

model <- cmdstan_model("R/completion_player.stan")
fit_stan <- model$sample(
  data = stan_data, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, seed = 431,
  iter_warmup = 1000, iter_sampling = 1000,
  adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12)

  variables = c("alpha", "tau", "theta", "s_rep", "s_test_rep"),

CmdStanR specifies warmup and sampling separately: iter_warmup = 1000 and iter_sampling = 1000 give 2,000 iterations per chain. Four chains therefore retain 4,000 posterior draws in total. Warmup adapts the sampler and is excluded from posterior summaries. adapt_delta sets the target acceptance probability used in adaptation. max_treedepth limits NUTS trajectory expansion.

title: 4.5 Bayesian Player Models in Stan
text:
8 Held-out log posterior predictive density
Choose Patrick Mahomes’s first included game after Week 10. Let S*S_* denote completions in that game and n*n_* its attempt count. Given training outcomes 𝒚\mathbf y, the predictive distribution is
P(S*=s∣𝒚,n*)=∫Binomial⁡(s∣n*,θj)p(θj∣𝒚)dθj,s=0,…,n*.
P(S_*=s\mid\mathbf y,n_*)
=\int \operatorname{Binomial}(s\mid n_*,\theta_j)\,
       p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)\,d\theta_j,
\qquad s=0,\ldots,n_*.

Here jj indexes Mahomes and ss is a possible future completion count. The posterior for θj\theta_j already integrates over α\alpha and τ\tau. For draw mm, simulate S*rep,(m)∼Binomial⁡(n*,θj(m))S_*^{\mathrm{rep},(m)}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_*,\theta_j^{(m)}). The Stan program does this in generated quantities; it uses no held-out completions to update the posterior.
For predictive evaluation, let s*s_* be the observed completion count in this held-out game. The log posterior predictive score is
ℓ*=log⁡P(S*=s*∣𝒚,n*)=log⁡Eθj∣𝒚[Binomial(s*∣n*,θj)]≈log⁡[1M∑m=1MBinomial(s*∣n*,θj(m))].
\begin{aligned}
\ell_*&=\log P(S_*=s_*\mid\mathbf y,n_*)\\
&=\log E_{\theta_j\mid\mathbf y}
  \left[\operatorname{Binomial}(s_*\mid n_*,\theta_j)\right]\\
&\approx\log\left[\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}
  \operatorname{Binomial}(s_*\mid n_*,\theta_j^{(m)})\right].
\end{aligned}

Here ℓ*\ell_* is one game’s log score, MM is the number of retained posterior draws, and mm indexes those draws. The notation Binomial⁡(s*∣n*,θj)\operatorname{Binomial}(s_*\mid n_*,\theta_j) means the probability mass (n*s*)θjs*(1−θj)n*−s*\binom{n_*}{s_*}\theta_j^{s_*}(1-\theta_j)^{n_*-s_*}. Because completion counts are discrete, we evaluate a probability mass, although the conventional name is log posterior predictive density.
Average the probability masses over posterior draws, then take the natural logarithm. This integrates uncertainty about player probability. It generally differs from averaging the log probability masses or inserting a single posterior mean probability into the binomial formula. Stan held-out evaluation guidance

8.1 Scores across held-out games
One game’s score illustrates the calculation. For comparing predictive models, evaluate all the same held-out games. Let GtestG_{\mathrm{test}} be their number, gg index a held-out quarterback-game row, sgs_g its observed completions, ngn_g its attempts, and j(g)j(g) its quarterback. Define the sum of game-wise log predictive scores as
LPDtest=∑g=1Gtestlog⁡P(Sg=sg∣𝒚,ng,j(g)).
\mathrm{LPD}_{\mathrm{test}}
=\sum_{g=1}^{G_{\mathrm{test}}}
\log P(S_g=s_g\mid\mathbf y,n_g,j(g)).

Here SgS_g is the random completion count for row gg, and LPDtest\mathrm{LPD}_{\mathrm{test}} denotes the total held-out log predictive score. Each game’s predictive probability uses the training posterior, with no updating on earlier held-out outcomes. This is a sum of marginal game scores, rather than the log probability of the entire held-out dataset jointly.

    x = test$completions[g], size = test$attempts[g],
    prob = post_stan$theta[, qb_index[g]], log = TRUE)

Compare alternatives, such as complete pooling versus partial pooling, using the same training/test split, outcomes, and aggregation unit. Higher total or mean log scores indicate better predictive performance on that test set. A comparison between CmdStanR and rstanarm fits with matching likelihoods and priors primarily checks implementation agreement. Small Monte Carlo differences do not establish a better statistical model.
The held-out average estimates expected log predictive performance for similar future games. The term expected log predictive density (ELPD) refers to averaging the log predictive score over future outcomes. A held-out upper-tail probability, P(S*rep≥s*∣𝒚,n*)P(S_*^{\mathrm{rep}}\ge s_*\mid\mathbf y,n_*), can help identify an unusually low observed count, but it is not a score to maximize when comparing models. A model that consistently predicts too many completions can have large upper-tail probabilities. Keep the predictive plot and interval for interpretation, and use log predictive scores for comparison. The training-data Bayesian p-value below checks a particular feature of the model.

9 Posterior predictive checks and a Bayesian p-value
To check a model, simulate replicated training outcomes from posterior draws, retaining the observed game attempt counts. Compare a statistic of these replications with the same statistic of the observed training data.
Use Mahomes’s variation in completion rates across training games. For his GjG_j training games, define rg=Sg/ngr_g=S_g/n_g and their unweighted mean r‾=Gj−1∑grg\bar r=G_j^{-1}\sum_g r_g. Our discrepancy statistic is
T(𝑺)=1Gj−1∑g=1Gj(rg−r‾)2,
T(\mathbf S)=\frac{1}{G_j-1}\sum_{g=1}^{G_j}(r_g-\bar r)^2,

where 𝑺\mathbf S is the vector of his game completion counts and the sums run over his training games. The replicated statistic uses simulated counts and the same attempt counts. This checks game-to-game variation beyond what the constant-probability model predicts, rather than merely checking the fitted total completions.
The posterior predictive Bayesian p-value is
pB=P(T(𝑺rep)≥T(𝑺)∣𝒚)≈1M∑m=1MI[T(𝑺rep,(m))≥T(𝑺)].
p_B=P\!\left(T(\mathbf S^{\mathrm{rep}})\ge T(\mathbf S)\mid\mathbf y\right)
\approx\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}
 I\!\left[T(\mathbf S^{\mathrm{rep},(m)})\ge T(\mathbf S)\right].

Here 𝒚\mathbf y is all training data used to fit the hierarchy; MM is the number of retained draws; I[A]I[A] equals 1 when statement AA holds and 0 otherwise; and 𝑺rep,(m)\mathbf S^{\mathrm{rep},(m)} is a simulated training-game count vector at draw mm.

check_rows <- which(train$passer == "Patrick Mahomes")
check_attempts <- train$attempts[check_rows]
T_observed <- game_dispersion(train$completions[check_rows], check_attempts)
T_replicated <- game_dispersion(post_stan$s_rep[, check_rows, drop = FALSE],
                               check_attempts)
p_B <- mean(T_replicated >= T_observed)
data.frame(statistic = "Variance of Mahomes's training-game completion rates",
           observed = T_observed, replicated_mean = mean(T_replicated),
           Bayesian_p_value = p_B) %>% knitr::kable(digits = 4)

A Bayesian p-value is not the probability that the model is true. Because the training data both fit and check the model, these p-values are not generally uniform under a correct model and should not automatically be read against a frequentist 0.05 cutoff. title: 4.5 Bayesian Player Models in Stan
text:
11 Key takeaways

A full Bayesian player model includes priors for unknown population parameters.
Custom Stan through cmdstanr and formula-based rstanarm can fit the same model when their likelihoods and priors match.
Sampling diagnostics establish computational reliability; predictive checks examine the model’s implications.
A posterior predictive distribution includes parameter uncertainty and future outcome randomness.
Held-out log predictive scores evaluate probability assigned to observed outcomes. Compare models across the same held-out games, with higher scores indicating better predictive performance.
A posterior predictive Bayesian p-value is a statistic-specific model check, separate from held-out predictive evaluation.
